fixed.review_text:
The code has three security vulnerabilities. The state-changing transaction actions are reachable with only debugging access, and the forms that trigger them provide no CSRF protection.

**1. Broken access control (CWE-285)**
File: `twopcz.go`, line 135
```
if err := acl.CheckAccessHTTP(r, acl.DEBUGGING); err != nil {
```
Commit, rollback, discard, and conclude all run after this single `acl.DEBUGGING` check (lines 142–148). Those calls change prepared and distributed transactions. The handler itself warns that they can jeopardize data integrity (line 184), but the code never requires a stricter admin role.

**2. Cross-site request forgery (CWE-352)**
File: `twopcz.go`, lines 140–141
```
dtid := r.FormValue("dtid")
action := r.FormValue("Action")
```
`FormValue` accepts query parameters and the body, and the handler never checks `r.Method` or a CSRF token before calling `RollbackPrepared`, `CommitPrepared`, or `ConcludeTransaction`. The forms that submit those actions also omit `method` (so they default to GET) and any anti-CSRF token:

File: `twopcz.go`, lines 81–83
```
<form>
    <input type="hidden" name="dtid" value="{{.Dtid}}"></input>
    <input type="submit" name="Action" value="Discard"></input>
```
The same pattern appears at lines 102–105 (Rollback/Commit) and 126–128 (Conclude). A browser that already satisfies the ACL can be made to trigger those actions. Mutation also happens before the `format` branch, so a JSON GET performs the same state change.

**3. Clickjacking (CWE-1021)**
File: `twopcz.go`, line 183
```
w.Write(gridTable)
```
The HTML response is written with no `X-Frame-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors`. Combined with the one-click commit, rollback, and conclude forms above, the page can be framed and the buttons activated by a click on a decoy UI.

The template output and the status string are escaped (`safehtml/template`, `html.EscapeString` on line 186), so no XSS was found in this file.

vuln.review_text:
**twopcz.go:185 — Reflected XSS (CWE-79).** `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` writes `msg` into an HTML response with no escaping. `msg` is built from request data at lines 152 and 154 (`r.FormValue("Action")` and `dtid`). `Action` is echoed even when it is not one of the switch cases, and `dtid` is attacker-controlled. The `safehtml` templates do not cover this path. HTML starts at line 182, so a debugging user who opens a crafted URL executes the payload.

**twopcz.go:141 — CSRF / state change via GET (CWE-352).** The handler applies `Discard`, `Rollback`, `Commit`, and `Conclude` from `r.FormValue` with no CSRF token, no `Origin` check, and no `r.Method` restriction. `FormValue` honors query parameters, so a GET is enough. The forms at lines 80, 101, and 125 omit `method`, so they default to GET and send no token (`<td><form>`). A site that can cause a browser to request this URL can commit, roll back, or conclude a transaction for an already-authenticated debugging user. Basic auth is resent automatically on same-origin requests.

**twopcz.go:134 — Weak authorization for integrity-critical actions (CWE-285).** `acl.CheckAccessHTTP(r, acl.DEBUGGING)` is the only gate, and it covers both the read view and the mutations at lines 143–147. Those calls (`RollbackPrepared`, `CommitPrepared`, `ConcludeTransaction`) can change transaction outcomes; the page itself warns they can jeopardize data integrity. Debug-level access is broader than what these actions need.

**twopcz.go:159 — Sensitive error disclosure (CWE-209).** `http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)` returns raw internal errors to the client (same pattern at line 174, and again inside `msg` at line 152).

The `safehtml/template` row templates (lines 75–85, 96–107, 119–130) contextually escape `.Dtid`, `.Queries`, and the other fields; those writes are not XSS. Static fragments (`gridTable`, headers) are constants.
